title: How AI Ideas Affect the Creativity, Diversity, and Evolution of Human Ideas: Evidence From a Large, Dynamic Experiment
author: Joshua Ashkinaze · Julia Mendelsohn · Li Qiwei · Ceren Budak · Eric Gilbert

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source studies passive exposure to AI-generated ideas and its effects on creativity and collective diversity, not legal workflows, verification, lawyer replacement or professional competence. Its findings that effects vary by task, person and mode of interaction are broadly compatible with the cluster’s emphasis on bounded, context-dependent effects, but do not establish a position on the cluster’s principal legal-workflow proposition.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source reinforces the cluster’s distinction between bounded effects and general competence, while materially extending it with dynamic evidence that deployment design, exposure level, disclosure and user characteristics shape outcomes. It shows that AI exposure can increase collective idea diversity without improving individual originality, underscoring the need to select use cases and outcome measures carefully; however, its passive creativity task does not directly establish effects in legal work.

st.t: Creative diversity: Individual gains can homogenise groups
st.an: The source supports the synthesis’s separation of individual creativity from collective diversity and its rejection of inevitable homogenisation. In its passive-exposure setting, high AI exposure increased collective diversity while leaving average individual creativity unchanged, showing that diversity effects depend on task and interaction design.

st.t: Practical productivity: AI can save or consume time
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s task- and outcome-specific framing by showing that AI exposure can increase collective idea diversity while not establishing improved individual creativity or general productivity. Its dynamic response-chain design also reinforces the need to measure cumulative, collective effects separately from immediate individual performance.

kp.k: Dynamic brainstorming experiment separates exposure from disclosure
kp.d: This cross-domain study examines brainstorming rather than legal work. The supplied manuscript is arXiv:2401.13481v3, dated 31 July 2025, with a CI 2025 publication reference, notwithstanding the document heading's 2024 designation. The experiment collected 3414 analyzed responses from 844 participants across 48 countries. Participants generated one creative use for each of five objects, encountering every experimental condition once: six human examples, two AI and four human examples, or four AI and two human examples, with AI examples either labeled or unlabeled. Human responses fed forward within condition–item combinations; chains were intended to reset after 20 responses, with seven replications per combination.
qs: Our experiment manipulates two key factors:
Neither items nor conditions repeat in a 5-trial sequence.
These ‘response chains’ reset every 20 responses.

kp.k: Exposure concerns existing outputs, not interactive AI collaboration
kp.d: The authors distinguish seeing AI-generated ideas from actively creating outputs with AI. They generated examples using ChatGPT-3.5 and zero-shot prompting, modifying the prompt to approximate human response lengths and prevent length from revealing source identity. AI did not receive the examples shown to humans. Although framed as passive exposure, participants ranked examples before submitting ideas, a step explicitly intended to ensure engagement. Accordingly, the study concerns exposure to pre-generated examples rather than interactive co-creation or wholly incidental viewing.
qs: users see LLM outputs but do not have an active role in the creation of these
Rank them by creativity.
We chose ChatGPT-3.5 for ecological validity
We chose not to vary prompts

kp.k: Originality, diversity, and adoption are distinct measured outcomes
kp.d: Individual creativity was operationalized as originality predicted by an existing fine-tuned GPT-3 classifier, not as creativity in all its dimensions. Its reported overall correlation with human judgments was r = 0.81; the five chosen objects had correlations of 0.88–0.91. SBERT embeddings measured collective diversity through median pairwise cosine distance and local diversity through distance between submitted ideas and examples. AI adoption meant maximum cosine similarity to an AI example, an operational proxy rather than direct evidence of intentional copying. Distance and similarity outcomes were multiplied by 100 for interpretation.
qs: we focus on originality.
AI adoption is the maximum cosine similarity
All ideas embedded using SBERT.
we scale the dependent variable (cosine distance or cosine similarity, respectively) by 100 for easier interpretation.

kp.k: High exposure increases collective diversity, not measured creativity
kp.d: Both high-exposure conditions increased global diversity relative to control: Cliff’s delta was 0.31 with disclosure and 0.26 without disclosure, each with adjusted p = 0.001. In contrast, conditions did not significantly differ in individual originality, F(4, 19.86) = 0.12, p = 0.97, or its temporal evolution, likelihood-ratio χ²(4) = 6.52, p = 0.16. Local diversity also showed no main condition effect, F(4, 19.95) = 0.09, p = 0.98. These are task-specific null findings, not proof that AI cannot influence creativity elsewhere.
qs: AI made ideas different, not better.
Seeing AI ideas does not affect creativity
the results are directionally similar.

kp.k: Low-exposure findings contain an unresolved reporting discrepancy
kp.d: Section 5.2 identifies low exposure without disclosure as producing a small increase in global diversity, delta = 0.11 and p = 0.001. However, supplementary Table 12 assigns that increase to low exposure with disclosure, reporting a mean difference of 0.47, adjusted p = 0.001 and delta = 0.11; its undisclosed condition instead has a difference of −0.61, adjusted p = 0.0063 and delta = −0.06. The high-exposure finding is consistent across these locations, but the low-exposure condition labels and direction cannot be reconciled from the supplied text.

kp.k: High exposure changes diversity's trajectory across successive responses
kp.d: Control-condition diversity declined across trials, β = −0.39, 95% CI [−0.73, −0.05], p = 0.03. Relative to that control slope, the high-exposure slope was more positive without disclosure, β = 0.53, 95% CI [0.06, 0.99], p = 0.03, and with disclosure, β = 0.57, 95% CI [0.1, 1.03], p = 0.02. Low-exposure slopes did not significantly differ from control. The temporal analysis excluded the first six trials to reduce seed effects and controlled for pool size. These results describe experimental iterations, not measured long-term societal change.
qs: High exposure to AI ideas increased the rate of change in idea diversity.
we only ran this analysis on data after the sixth trial in a response chain to rule out the effect of seeds on evolution.

kp.k: Disclosure moderates adoption differently by self-perceived creativity
kp.d: The abstract reports no main disclosure effects, but subgroup analysis finds disclosure moderated the exposure–adoption relationship among participants low in self-perceived creativity. Comparing the top and bottom deciles, the difference between exposure effects under undisclosed and disclosed conditions was nonsignificant for the high-creativity group, Δ = −1.69, d = −0.14, p = 0.59, but significant for the low-creativity group, Δ = 7.77, d = 0.65, p = 0.03. These categories reflect self-assessment, not independently established creative ability. The authors do not interpret adoption's main exposure effect because maximum similarity can increase mechanically when more AI examples are available.
qs: There were no main effects of disclosure.
People who identify as creative are less influenced by AI disclosure.
we would expect higher similarity to AI ideas in the high-exposure condition by chance

kp.k: Greater adoption on difficult prompts remains speculative
kp.d: For high exposure, the rank-order correlation between task difficulty and AI adoption was ρ = 0.8 when AI ideas were disclosed, versus ρ = 0.3 when undisclosed. Difficulty was inferred from lower average originality in control responses, rather than independently manipulated. The authors explicitly treat this five-object result as speculative. They suggest AI may support people when stuck and raise the conditional possibility that routine reliance could contribute to model collapse; the experiment does not test model training or collapse.
qs: Participants may adopt AI ideas more for harder prompts.
this finding should be taken as
speculative (due to the small number of items) and not conclusive.
We measure the ‘difficulty’ of a prompt by the inverse rank of the average creativity in the control condition.

kp.k: AI idea banks may interrupt collective convergence
kp.d: The authors propose that injecting AI examples partially resets convergence along human idea sequences. They suggest that collective brainstorming may therefore differ from individual interactive co-creation, potentially explaining why this study finds increased diversity while some prior studies find homogenization. This is a proposed mechanism and boundary condition, not a demonstrated general solution to groupthink. Whether increased diversity without increased average originality generates innovation is left as a future research question.
qs: AI’s effect on ideas may depend on whether it’s used
for individual ideation versus collective brainstorming.
can this dynamic generate “innovation”?

kp.k: Generalization is limited by task, sample, and implementation
kp.d: The study uses one brainstorming task, five objects, one model and prompting approach, and a nonrepresentative volunteer sample emphasizing technology-interested users and creative professionals. Originality scores inherit classifier error and do not establish effects on fluency or elaboration. The authors describe their cultural-evolution model as stylized and recommend other tasks, models, prompts, measurement approaches and transmission scenarios. Implementation qualifications include some profane examples reaching participants before moderation, 38 excluded responses from 3452 initially collected, and chains ranging from 14 to 24 responses rather than uniformly 20. Trial feedback sometimes used an arbitrary random number when a metric could not be calculated.
qs: our sample also limits generalizability.
future work could explore more complex transmission scenarios.
The maximum number of trials was 24.
we returned an arbitrary, random number.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Ashkinaze and colleagues claim that high exposure to AI-generated brainstorming examples increases collective idea diversity without measurably improving individual originality, with effects on adoption varying by self-perceived creativity and task difficulty.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain study of creative brainstorming, not legal services. The authors report that high AI exposure increased collective semantic diversity and made its trajectory more positive relative to human-only examples. They found no significant condition differences in individual creativity or its temporal evolution. They report no main effects of disclosure, while identifying a subgroup interaction: labeling examples as AI-generated reduced the effect of exposure on adoption among participants with low self-perceived creativity, but not among those with high self-perceived creativity. They also suggest, explicitly speculatively, that people may knowingly adopt AI ideas more for difficult prompts. Their proposed mechanism is that introducing AI examples interrupts convergence among successive human contributions. Broader suggestions that this could counter groupthink, produce cumulative cultural effects, or contribute to model collapse through routine reliance are interpretations or conditional possibilities, not directly established outcomes.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal claims rest on a randomized, dynamic online experiment with 844 participants and 3,414 analyzed responses; broader mechanisms and consequences remain interpretive.
pts.d: Participants from 48 countries generated alternative uses for five objects after viewing six examples. Conditions included zero, two, or four AI examples, with AI source labels either disclosed or undisclosed. Human responses fed forward within condition-and-item response chains. The design targeted seven chains per item-condition combination, with approximately 20 responses per chain. Creativity was measured using an existing fine-tuned GPT-3 originality classifier, with reported correlations against human judgments of 0.88–0.91 for the selected objects; diversity was measured using SBERT semantic distances. High-exposure collective-diversity effects versus control were Cliff’s delta 0.31 with disclosure and 0.26 without disclosure, both adjusted p = 0.001. The control diversity slope was −0.39; high-exposure slope differences relative to control were +0.53 without disclosure and +0.57 with disclosure. Individual creativity did not differ significantly by condition (p = 0.97), and adding condition-specific temporal evolution did not significantly improve model fit (p = 0.16). Adoption was operationalized as maximum semantic similarity to AI examples, not directly observed copying or conscious reliance. The authors acknowledge that more AI examples can mechanically raise maximum similarity and therefore emphasize subgroup contrasts rather than adoption main effects. The disclosure-by-exposure contrast was significant for low self-perceived creativity (d = 0.65, p = 0.03), not high self-perceived creativity (p = 0.59). The difficulty finding rests on correlations across only five objects. An internal reporting discrepancy should be preserved: section 5.2 identifies low-exposure undisclosed examples as producing a small diversity increase, whereas supplementary Table 12 assigns the positive delta of 0.11 to low-exposure disclosed examples and reports a negative delta for low-exposure undisclosed examples.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The measured changes occur over short experimental response chains using ChatGPT-3.5 examples; long-run cultural consequences are extrapolations rather than longitudinal findings.
pts.d: Although the supplied heading identifies the source as 2024, the document itself is arXiv v3 dated 31 July 2025 and cites the August 2025 Collective Intelligence Conference. Implementation notes reference July 2023. Experimental time means successive contributions within response chains, not months or years of changes in individual ability. Global and diversity-evolution analyses exclude the first six chain positions to reduce seed effects. AI stimuli were generated through a length-constrained zero-shot prompt using ChatGPT-3.5; humans, unlike the model generating stimuli, saw prior examples. The authors frame this as passive exposure rather than interactive AI co-creation, although participants were required to rank examples before submitting their own idea and were informed generally that examples could include AI. Findings concern one short alternative-use response per object and originality rather than all dimensions of creativity. Generalization to other models, prompting strategies, complex tasks, active collaboration, or real-world cultural transmission is left to future research. No specific calendar forecast is offered for cumulative effects, innovation, or model collapse.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly studied population comprises volunteer brainstormers, especially creativity- and technology-interested users; the proposed wider relevance concerns groups and the public encountering AI-generated ideas.
pts.d: The authors recruited unpaid adult volunteers through Reddit, Creative Mornings, Facebook advertisements, and shared links. Creative Mornings supplied 40.6% of participants and r/InternetIsBeautiful supplied 35.3%. This was a non-representative sample rather than a general-population probability sample. At the individual level, participants showed no detected improvement or deterioration in classifier-scored originality. At the collective level, high AI exposure produced a more semantically varied pool of human ideas and a more positive diversity trajectory. Participants with lower self-perceived creativity were more responsive to AI source disclosure in the exposure-adoption relationship; this distinction concerns self-assessment, not independently established creative expertise. Participants facing harder prompts may have relied more on labeled AI ideas, but that interpretation remains tentative. The authors extend the relevance to collective thought and everyday encounters with AI content, without testing effects on legal professionals, clients, legal markets, employment, or service quality.
